title: Module Implementation Reference
readerIntent: Create, inspect, extend, and validate a Nodics module using the standard ownership and loader contracts.
priorKnowledge: Understand layered architecture, configuration, schemas, services, APIs, testing, and documentation.
owner: nConfig module metadata/loading and the concrete module that owns each contribution
summary: A Nodics module is a package-defined ownership boundary with canonical metadata, layered configuration, loader-visible source contributions, owned data/tests/docs, and later-layer customization—not merely a folder or server.

sections.heading: Placement checklist
items: Identify reusable framework responsibility versus customer-project business responsibility and choose the group accordingly.
Confirm the module can own its schemas, services, routes, properties, lifecycle, tests, and documentation without duplicating another authority.
Keep package metadata minimal, behavior in properties.js, and provider integrations behind existing gateways.
Validate monoServer composition and independent modular execution where the module contract supports both.

sections.heading: Required root contract
items: package.json: standard package identity/dependencies plus the minimal package.json.nodics metadata contract.
nodics.js: module lifecycle entrypoint used by Nodics startup/loading.
AGENTS.md: local AI/developer behavior and ownership rules.
README.md: concise human purpose, ownership, configuration, extension, operations, verification, and canonical-documentation links.
config/properties.js, prescripts.js, and postscripts.js: mandatory layered extension points, even when intentionally empty.
llm/README.md and generated module context for module-shaped packages except the designated setup authority.

sections.heading: Metadata
items: package.json.name is the canonical runtime identifier; established identifiers require explicit compatibility migration before rename.
package.json.nodics.kind classifies application, group, environment, server, node, module, or other supported boundary; never infer kind from the folder name or n-prefix.
package.json.nodics.runtime and runtimeModule are the runtime/loader flags; package.json.nodics.owns declares owned source surfaces.
Parent, required, index, dependency, and composition metadata establish deterministic hierarchy and load order.
Runtime policy, permissions, navigation, endpoints, provider selection, limits, feature switches, and BackOffice presentation belong in layered properties.js, not package.json.
Do not introduce a parallel manifest or duplicate metadata name.

sections.heading: Source ownership
items: src/schemas/schemas.js: item definitions, relationships, access, generation, cache/event/transaction, persistence, and search alignment.
src/router/routers.js and appConfig.js: route and HTTP application contributions.
src/controller: transport mapping only; src/facade: orchestration; src/service: business/provider/tooling behavior.
src/pipelines/pipelines.js: pipeline registry; src/event/listeners.js: listener definitions; src/interceptors: validation/lifecycle interception.
src/search/indexes.js: owned search indexes; src/utils: mergeable utilities, enums, and status definitions; src/lib: class-based libraries.
data/init is mandatory bootstrap only; data/core and data/sample are explicit imports. Pure groups and project roots do not own empty data folders.
test contains behavior owned by that layer. docs contains permanent local technical references and is excluded from runtime module discovery.

sections.heading: Implementation and customization
items: Search existing authorities and extension points first; reuse, then customize, and create new behavior last.
Keep runtime files inside loader radar and export mergeable members so later modules can replace one behavior without copying the whole file.
Use named configurable policies instead of closure constants or hardcoded project roles/servers/tenants/providers.
Generated blank defaultSampleService.js is an optional module-creation placeholder only. It must remain empty and is never a required service or business-logic owner.
Do not hand-edit generated controllers, facades, services, models, tests, documentation projections, or context when their source definition/generator owns them.
Keep customer business logic in customer project modules and frontend renderers in client repositories.

sections.heading: Definition of done
items: Metadata, parent/index, dependencies, ownership, configuration defaults/overrides, source map, permissions, tenancy, lifecycle, observability, performance, migration, deployment, and failure/recovery are explicit.
Positive, negative, boundary, contract, integration, customization/override, topology, security, performance, upgrade, generated-artifact, and regression tests pass as applicable.
Canonical user/developer documentation and concise module README match implementation; AGENTS and generated context express the same ownership rules.
Package and application dependencies remain synchronized with the root dependency-governance contract.
Structure, metadata, copyright, documentation, LLM/context, focused, baseline, and release gates report exact evidence and limitations.

sections.heading: Complete guide: Complete Module Catalog
paragraphs: This catalog makes every package-defined Nodics module reachable from the public documentation. It is an inventory and navigation aid, not a second source of module identity or behavior. The module package metadata and its README remain authoritative.
Use the [Module Documentation Index](/docs/reference/modules) when you know the business or platform task. Use this catalog when you know a module, group, environment, server, or node name.

sections.heading: Complete guide: Module Documentation Index
paragraphs: This page helps you move from task-based documentation in `gDocs` to the capability-specific documentation owned by each Nodics module.

Use `gDocs` when you want to understand a feature from the user or application developer perspective. Use module `README.md` files when you need exact source definitions, extension points, services, routers, schemas, pipelines, configuration, tests, and module-owned behavior.

Use the [Provider And Capability Maturity Matrix](/docs/reference/maturity) before selecting a provider or external adapter. It shows whether a capability is production-ready, guarded, sample/reference, scaffolded, or parked for later work.

This page is a task-oriented capability map. Use the [Complete Module Catalog](/docs/reference/modules) when you need to find every package-defined module, including application, environment, server, and node composition modules that are not appropriate in a short capability map.

sections.heading: How To Read A Module README
paragraphs: Module documentation is more detailed than public task guides because it tells you exactly how one capability works. When reading a module README, look for answers to these beginner questions:

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| What capability does this module own? | Prevents code from being added to the wrong module. |
| Which schemas, routes, services, facades, controllers, pipelines, interceptors, events, data, and tests does it own? | Shows which layer should receive the change. |
| Which configuration values belong to this module? | Keeps policy and provider choices out of hardcoded services. |
| How can a project override or extend the behavior? | Protects framework immutability and customer customization. |
| Which generated artifacts depend on this module? | Shows when to run build, generated tests, OpenAPI, or LLM generation. |
| Which tests prove the default and override behavior? | Gives developers and AI tools a verification path. |
If a module README does not answer these questions clearly enough, update the module README as part of the change. Do not make a beginner or AI tool infer the extension path from source code alone.

sections.heading: Documentation Ownership Rule
paragraphs: If a page explains how a user performs a task, it belongs in `gDocs`.
If a page explains the exact behavior owned by one module, its concise orientation belongs in the module `README.md` and its detailed guidance belongs in the canonical documentation content pack.
If a page defines rules that AI tools and developers must follow while changing code, it belongs in `AGENTS.md` or `gSetup/llm`.
